status: drafted directly (single-pass) following the established Genesis-through-Deuteronomy/Matthew methodology, then adversarially fact-checked; four real issues found and corrected in this pass: (1) missing naming-collision flag on "Antipas" (Rev 2:13) vs. Herod Antipas of Matthew.json, (2) the Two Witnesses reclassified from a law/theme tier to a full person-type manager tier per this project's own embodiment test, (3) the previously-merged "guiding angel" submanager split into two distinct entries reflecting a real textual distinction (the unspecified "his angel" of 1:1/22:6 vs. the explicitly-named "one of the seven angels which had the seven vials" of 17:1/19:9-10/21:9/22:8-9), and (4) the "Son of man" harvest-reaper of 14:14-16 cross-referenced into Jesus's own manager entry, consistent with how his other title-based appearances were already duplicated there.
notes: Revelation is the Bible's one sustained apocalyptic/visionary NT book, so its scribe tiers follow the same law/vision-tier approach used for Daniel's and Ezekiel's visions in the OT rather than treating every image as a person: most of the book's structural content (the seven letters, the seven seals, seven trumpets, seven bowls, and the closing sequence of judgment/restoration visions) are law-type tiers named around the actual content, each attributed via "deliveredBy" - the seven letters to Jesus Christ himself as the direct speaker ("These things saith he..."), and the remaining visions to John as the one who received, witnessed, and recorded them for the churches (Rev 1:1-2, 1:11). Six figures/entities are personally embodied enough across the book's own action (they act, suffer, decide, and are physically changed by events, not merely relay content) to warrant full person-type manager tiers: John himself (present, instructed, and physically responsive throughout, from Patmos in ch1 to his own closing testimony in ch22); Jesus Christ, given his own independent Revelation-specific tier per this project's established Gospel-book rule, since his portrayal here (Son of man among the candlesticks, the slain-yet-standing Lamb, the conquering rider on the white horse) is wholly distinct from his four Gospel tiers; the book's central antagonist trio - Satan/the Dragon, the Beast from the sea, and the False Prophet (the beast from the earth) - each of whom acts, is bound or captured, and is finally judged across multiple chapters, unlike the vision-imagery that surrounds them; and, on adversarial-review correction, the Two Witnesses (11:3-12), who prophesy, are killed, lie unburied, and are bodily resurrected and taken up in full public view - a narrative arc at least as embodied as the antagonist trio, so they are now a collective person-type manager tier rather than a law tier, kept as ONE collective entry since the text never differentiates their individual actions. Naming/identity flags: "that woman Jezebel" of Thyatira (2:20) is explicitly NOT the same person as Ahab's wife Jezebel from 1-2 Kings, who lived roughly nine centuries earlier - the text's own chosen label for a local false prophetess, not a claim of identity. "Antipas" (2:13), the church's martyr at Pergamos, is explicitly NOT the same person as Herod Antipas, the tetrarch of Galilee already indexed under Matthew.json (who executed John the Baptist) - two unrelated men sharing a name, flagged per this project's naming-collision rule. The seer is named only "John" (1:1, 1:9) - the traditional identification with the Apostle John, author of the fourth Gospel, is noted as tradition only and never asserted as textual fact, per this project's later/traditional-name rule. The popular identification of the Two Witnesses with Moses and Elijah is logged in genealogyLists as tradition, not textual fact. The text draws a real distinction between two angelic guide references that were previously merged into one entry: the unspecified "his angel" of 1:1 and 22:6, versus the angel explicitly and repeatedly identified as "one of the seven angels which had the seven vials" at 17:1 and 21:9, who guides John through the judgment of Babylon and the vision of the New Jerusalem (17:1-19:10, 21:9-22:9) - now split into two separate submanager entries under John rather than one blended, uncertain identity. Balaam (2:14) is a reference back to the figure already indexed in Numbers.json, not a new character - id disambiguated as "balaam_revelation". Satan's dragon id is disambiguated as "satan_revelation" to avoid any future collision with a Job.json entry, since Job's "Satan/the Adversary" is a separate indexing context even though Rev 12:9 itself explicitly links "that old serpent" back to Genesis. Jesus's manager entry now also includes 14:14-16 ("one like unto the Son of man" reaping the harvest with a sickle) cross-referenced from the "everlasting_gospel_and_harvest" law tier, since it reuses the identical "Son of man" title John applies to the risen Christ at 1:13 - consistent with how the Lamb's other title-based appearances (opening the seals, receiving worship) were already duplicated into Jesus's own manager entry elsewhere in this file. The book's final tier, covering the new heaven, new earth, and New Jerusalem (21:1-22:21), is deliberately built as the weightiest closing tier in the whole 66-book index, closing the canon's own narrative arc from Eden's lost tree of life (Genesis 3:24) to its restoration (Rev 22:2).

scribeTiers.scribeName: The Woman Clothed with the Sun
The Marriage Supper of the Lamb

characters.name: John (the Revelator)

verses.note: The Revelation of Jesus Christ is signified by his angel unto his servant John, 'who bare record of the word of God, and of the testimony of Jesus Christ, and of all things that he saw.'
John identifies himself as 'your brother, and companion in tribulation,' exiled on the isle of Patmos 'for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ.'
John is 'in the Spirit on the Lord's day' and hears a voice commanding him to write what he sees in a book and send it to the seven churches.
On seeing the risen Christ, John 'fell at his feet as dead.'
John takes a little book from an angel's hand and eats it at the angel's command - sweet as honey in his mouth, bitter in his belly.
John falls down to worship the revealing angel and is rebuked: 'See thou do it not... worship God.'
An angel carries John away in the Spirit to a great and high mountain to show him the holy city, New Jerusalem, descending.
John again falls down to worship the angel and is corrected a second time.
John's own closing testimony warns against adding to or taking away from 'the words of the prophecy of this book.'

funFacts: Twice in the book John falls down to worship the revealing angel and is corrected both times (19:10, 22:8-9) - a repeated, deliberate detail in the text.

Tradition identifies this John with the Apostle John / author of the fourth Gospel, but Revelation's own text never makes that identification explicit - treated here as a traditional attribution, not a stated fact.

characters.name: Jesus Christ (Revelation)

verses.note: Introduced as 'the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth.'

Seen among seven golden candlesticks as 'one like unto the Son of man' - hair white as wool, eyes as flame of fire, feet like fine brass, a voice as many waters, seven stars in his right hand, a sharp two-edged sword out of his mouth.
'I am the first and the last: I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore... and have the keys of hell and of death.'
Announced as 'the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David,' then seen as a Lamb 'as it had been slain,' who takes the sealed scroll from the hand of him that sat on the throne.
The Lamb is worshipped by all creation as worthy 'to take the book, and to open the seals thereof.'
The Lamb personally opens each of the seven seals in turn.

'One like unto the Son of man' - the identical title John applies to the risen Christ at 1:13, cross-referenced here from the 'Sharp Sickle' law tier - is seen sitting on a white cloud with a golden crown, and reaps the earth's harvest with a sharp sickle at an angel's word.

Appears as the rider on the white horse - 'Faithful and True,' 'The Word of God,' with 'KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS' written on his vesture and thigh - treading the winepress of the wrath of God.
Defeats the beast, the false prophet, and the kings of the earth gathered against him.
In the New Jerusalem, 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it,' and 'the Lamb is the light thereof.'
'I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.'
'I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star.'
'Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.'

funFacts: Given his own independent manager tier here, distinct from his tiers in the four Gospels, per this project's established rule that each of Jesus's book-portrayals carries real separate narrative weight.
Titled both 'the Lion of the tribe of Juda' and 'a Lamb as it had been slain' within the same vision (5:5-6) - two contrasting images introduced back to back.

The 'Son of man' title used at his first appearance among the candlesticks (1:13) recurs at the harvest vision (14:14-16), which is presented in the text without an explicit re-identification - the title match is the basis for reading it as the same figure, not a restated name.
His human genealogy is not restated here; it is already indexed under Matthew's Gospel (Matthew 1:1-17).

characters.name: The Letter to Ephesus
characters.purpose: Commends the church's labor, patience, and rejection of false apostles and the deeds of the Nicolaitans, but rebukes it for abandoning its first love and calls it to repent and return to its earlier works, on pain of having its candlestick removed.

verses.note: Addressed 'unto the angel of the church of Ephesus.'
Commended for works, labor, patience, and testing 'them which say they are apostles, and are not.'
Rebuke: 'thou hast left thy first love.'
Called to repent and 'do the first works,' or Christ will 'remove thy candlestick out of his place.'
Commended for hating 'the deeds of the Nicolaitanes, which I also hate.'
Promise to him that overcometh: 'to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.'

characters.name: The Letter to Smyrna
characters.purpose: Addressed to a church suffering real poverty and tribulation, with no rebuke at all - only encouragement to remain faithful even unto death against coming imprisonment, in exchange for the crown of life and exemption from 'the second death.'

verses.note: 'I know thy works, and tribulation, and poverty, (but thou art rich)... the blasphemy of them which say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.'
'Thou shalt have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.'
Promise: 'he that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death.'

characters.name: The Letter to Pergamos
characters.purpose: Commends the church for holding fast Christ's name even where 'Satan's seat' is, and even after the martyrdom of Antipas, but rebukes it for tolerating those who hold the doctrine of Balaam and the doctrine of the Nicolaitans.

verses.note: 'I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is... Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth.'
Rebuke for tolerating 'the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed unto idols, and to commit fornication.'
Also rebuked for those 'that hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitanes.'
Called to repent.
Promise: 'hidden manna,' and 'a white stone, and in the stone a new name written.'

characters.name: The Letter to Thyatira
characters.purpose: Commends growing works of charity, service, faith, and patience, but rebukes the church for tolerating 'that woman Jezebel' who taught and seduced Christ's servants into fornication and eating things sacrificed to idols, warning of severe judgment on her and her followers unless they repent.

verses.note: Commended: 'charity, and service, and faith, and thy patience, and thy works; and the last to be more than the first.'
Rebuke: the church suffers 'that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols.'
Given space to repent and refused; her and her 'children' (followers) threatened with great tribulation and death.
Those who 'have not known the depths of Satan' spared any further burden.
Promise to him that overcometh: power over the nations, and 'the morning star.'

characters.name: The Letter to Sardis
characters.purpose: A rebuke to a church with a reputation for life that is spiritually dead, urging it to be watchful and strengthen what remains, with a promise of white raiment and one's name kept in the book of life for the few who have 'not defiled their garments.'

verses.note: 'Thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead.'
Called to 'be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die.'
'Thou hast a few names even in Sardis which have not defiled their garments.'
Promise: 'clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life.'

characters.name: The Letter to Philadelphia
characters.purpose: Like Smyrna, receives no rebuke - commended for keeping Christ's word and not denying his name despite little strength, promised an 'open door' no man can shut and preservation 'from the hour of temptation, which shall come upon all the world.'

verses.note: 'Thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name... I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it.'
Those 'of the synagogue of Satan, which say they are Jews, and are not' made to bow before the church.
Promise to 'keep thee from the hour of temptation, which shall come upon all the world.'
Promise: made 'a pillar in the temple of my God,' written with the name of God, the New Jerusalem, and Christ's own new name.

characters.name: The Letter to Laodicea
characters.purpose: The most sharply rebuked of the seven - 'lukewarm' Laodicea is warned it will be 'spued' out of Christ's mouth, called wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked despite thinking itself rich; counseled to buy true riches from Christ, with the image of Christ standing at the door and knocking, and the promise of a shared throne to whoever opens.

verses.note: 'I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot... because thou art lukewarm... I will spue thee out of my mouth.'
'Thou sayest, I am rich... and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked.'
Counseled to buy gold tried in the fire, white raiment, and eyesalve.
'As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.'
'Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.'
Promise: 'to sit with me in my throne.'

characters.name: The Throne Room and the Sealed Scroll
characters.purpose: Shows the heavenly throne room itself - God enthroned, the four living creatures, the twenty-four elders, and a scroll sealed with seven seals that no one is found worthy to open until the slain-yet-standing Lamb takes it, establishing the vision's central image of worship before the action of the seals begins.

verses.note: A throne set in heaven, with one sitting on it 'like a jasper and a sardine stone.'
Twenty-four elders seated round about, clothed in white, with crowns of gold.
Four living creatures full of eyes, each with six wings, cry 'Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty.'
The elders' worship: 'Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power.'
A scroll sealed with seven seals; John weeps because 'no man was found worthy to open and to read the book.'
The Lamb, 'as it had been slain,' takes the book out of the right hand of him that sat on the throne.
All creation worships the Lamb: 'Worthy is the Lamb that was slain.'

characters.name: The Seven Seals
characters.purpose: The Lamb opens six of the seven seals in sequence, releasing the four horsemen (conquest, war, famine, death), the cry of martyred souls under the altar, and cosmic upheaval, building dread toward the seventh seal, which opens instead into silence and the trumpets to come.

verses.note: First seal: a white horse; its rider is given a crown and goes forth conquering.
Second seal: a red horse; its rider is given power to take peace from the earth.
Third seal: a black horse; its rider holds a pair of balances, signaling scarcity pricing.
Fourth seal: a pale horse; its rider is named Death, with Hell following, given power over a fourth of the earth.
Fifth seal: souls of the slain under the altar cry 'How long, O Lord,' are given white robes, and told to rest a little season.
Sixth seal: a great earthquake, the sun black, the moon as blood, stars falling, the sky departing, kings and great men hiding themselves.
Seventh seal: 'silence in heaven about the space of half an hour.'

characters.name: The 144,000 and the Great Multitude
characters.purpose: An interlude before the seventh seal's silence, sealing 144,000 servants of God - 12,000 from each of twelve tribes - followed by a vision of an uncountable multitude from every nation clothed in white with palms, who 'came out of great tribulation.'

verses.note: An angel seals 'the servants of our God in their foreheads'; the number sealed is 144,000.
Listed by tribe, 12,000 each (Dan is not named in this list, and both Joseph and Manasses appear).
'A great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations... clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands.'
'These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes... in the blood of the Lamb.'
'God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes.'

characters.name: The Seven Trumpets
characters.purpose: Seven angels sound seven trumpets in sequence, each unleashing an escalating plague on the earth, sea, rivers, and sky through demonic locusts and a vast army, building toward the seventh trumpet's declaration that 'the kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord.'

verses.note: First trumpet: hail and fire mingled with blood; a third of trees and all green grass burnt up.
Second trumpet: a burning mountain cast into the sea; a third of the sea becomes blood.
Third trumpet: a star named Wormwood falls, embittering a third of the rivers and fountains.
Fourth trumpet: a third of the sun, moon, and stars darkened.
Fifth trumpet: the bottomless pit is opened, releasing locusts with power like scorpions, ruled by 'a king... whose name in the Hebrew tongue is Abaddon, but in the Greek tongue... Apollyon.'
Sixth trumpet: four angels loosed from the river Euphrates lead an army of 200,000,000 that kills a third of mankind.
Seventh trumpet: 'The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ.'
The temple of God is opened in heaven, and the ark of his testament is seen.

characters.name: The Two Witnesses

verses.note: 'My two witnesses' are given power to prophesy 1,260 days in sackcloth, described as 'the two olive trees, and the two candlesticks standing before the God of the earth.'
Given power to devour enemies with fire from their mouth, to shut heaven so it does not rain, to turn waters to blood, and to smite the earth with plagues.
'The beast that ascendeth out of the bottomless pit shall make war against them, and shall overcome them, and kill them.'
Their bodies lie unburied 'in the street of the great city' for three and a half days.
After three and a half days, 'the Spirit of life from God entered into them,' they stand up, and ascend to heaven 'in a cloud' while their enemies watch.

funFacts: Reclassified from a law/theme tier to a full person-type manager tier on adversarial review: unlike the surrounding vision-imagery, the witnesses themselves act, suffer, are killed, lie exposed, and are bodily resurrected and taken up - the same personally-embodied standard used to justify full tiers for Satan, the Beast, and the False Prophet elsewhere in this book.
The text never names the two witnesses individually and does not differentiate their actions from one another - kept here as one collective entry rather than two invented individuals.

Popular tradition connects them to Moses and Elijah (the plague/fire/rain-stopping parallels), but the text itself does not make that identification - logged separately in genealogyLists as tradition, not textual fact.

characters.name: The Woman and the Dragon
characters.scribeTier: The Woman Clothed with the Sun
characters.purpose: A great sign-vision of a woman clothed with the sun, about to give birth, opposed by a great red dragon waiting to devour her child; when the child (who is 'to rule all nations with a rod of iron') is caught up to God's throne, the dragon is cast down to earth and pursues the woman, who is protected in the wilderness.

verses.note: 'A great wonder in heaven; a woman clothed with the sun... travailing in birth, and pained to be delivered.'
'A great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns,' whose tail draws a third of the stars of heaven, stands ready to devour her child.
She brings forth 'a man child, who was to rule all nations with a rod of iron,' and the child is 'caught up unto God, and to his throne.'
The woman flees into the wilderness, where she is fed 1,260 days.
The dragon persecutes the woman; she is given 'two wings of a great eagle,' nourished 'for a time, and times, and half a time.'
The dragon casts a flood of water after her; the earth helps the woman, swallowing the flood.
The dragon goes 'to make war with the remnant of her seed.'
'The great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world' - the text itself explicitly links this figure to the serpent of Genesis.
War in heaven: Michael and his angels fight against the dragon and his angels; the dragon loses, 'neither was their place found any more in heaven.'
Gives the beast 'his power, and his seat, and great authority'; men worship the dragon.
An unclean spirit 'like frogs' comes out of the mouth of the dragon, alongside the beast and the false prophet.
An angel 'laid hold on the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan, and bound him a thousand years.'
Cast into the bottomless pit and sealed, 'that he should deceive the nations no more, till the thousand years should be fulfilled.'
Loosed for a little season, he goes out to deceive the nations, 'Gog and Magog,' gathering them to battle.
Fire from God devours the gathered nations; the devil is 'cast into the lake of fire and brimstone... tormented day and night for ever and ever.'

characters.name: Michael the Archangel

verses.note: 'Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels.'

characters.perkNote: The only named angel to take direct combat action against Satan in the text; his role here is not elaborated beyond this single verse.

verses.note: Rises 'out of the sea, having seven heads and ten horns,' with a body like a leopard, feet like a bear, and mouth like a lion; the dragon gives him 'his power, and his seat, and great authority.'
One of his heads is 'as it were wounded to death; and his deadly wound was healed: and all the world wondered after the beast.'
Given 'a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies,' and power for forty-two months to blaspheme God, his name, and his tabernacle.
Given power 'to make war with the saints, and to overcome them,' and authority over all kindreds, tongues, and nations.
Worshipped by all whose names are not written in the Lamb's book of life.
Further described as 'was, and is not, and yet is,' with his seven heads further explained as both 'seven mountains' and 'seven kings.'
Captured together with the false prophet and 'cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone.'

characters.name: The False Prophet

verses.note: A second beast rises 'out of the earth,' having 'two horns like a lamb,' but speaking 'as a dragon.'
Exercises all the power of the first beast, causes the earth to worship it, does 'great wonders,' and makes fire come down from heaven.
Deceives the earth and tells them to make 'an image to the beast'; gives life and speech to the image and causes any who will not worship it to be killed.

Causes all, small and great, rich and poor, to receive 'a mark in their right hand, or in their foreheads,' without which none may buy or sell; the number of the beast is given as 'Six hundred threescore and six.'
Explicitly named 'the false prophet'; unclean spirits from his mouth gather kings to the battle of Armageddon.
Captured with the beast and 'cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone.'
Named alongside the beast, already in the lake of fire when the devil is cast in, 'tormented day and night for ever and ever.'

funFacts: First called simply 'another beast' rising out of the earth (13:11); only later (16:13) does the text explicitly give him the title 'the false prophet.'
The number 666 (13:18) is presented as an instruction to 'count' and identify the beast's name by number - the text does not itself state who or what this refers to.

characters.name: The Everlasting Gospel and the Harvest
characters.purpose: An interlude of three angelic proclamations - the everlasting gospel, the fall of Babylon foretold, and a warning against worshipping the beast or receiving his mark - followed by two harvest visions (grain and grapes) symbolizing final ingathering and judgment.

verses.note: The 144,000 seen again, standing with the Lamb on mount Sion, singing 'a new song' that only they can learn.
First angel: proclaims 'the everlasting gospel,' 'Fear God, and give glory to him; for the hour of his judgment is come.'
Second angel: 'Babylon is fallen, is fallen.'
Third angel: warns against worshipping the beast or receiving his mark.

One 'like unto the Son of man' seated on a cloud reaps the earth with a sickle - the grain harvest; this figure shares the exact 'Son of man' title used of the risen Christ at 1:13, cross-referenced into his own manager entry (jesus_revelation) rather than treated as a separate anonymous figure.
An angel gathers 'the vine of the earth' and casts it into 'the great winepress of the wrath of God,' trodden 'without the city.'

characters.name: The Seven Bowls of Wrath
characters.purpose: Seven angels pour out seven bowls ('vials' in the KJV) of God's wrath in rapid succession - sores, the sea and rivers turned to blood, scorching heat, darkness, the drying of the Euphrates to prepare the way for kings, and a final catastrophic earthquake - the most concentrated judgment sequence in the book, ending with the declaration 'It is done.'

verses.note: 'Seven angels having the seven last plagues; for in them is filled up the wrath of God.'
First vial: 'a noisome and grievous sore' falls upon those bearing the mark of the beast.
Second vial: the sea becomes blood, 'and every living soul died in the sea.'
Third vial: rivers and fountains of waters become blood.
Fourth vial: men are scorched with great heat from the sun.
Fifth vial: darkness falls upon the beast's kingdom.
Sixth vial: the river Euphrates is dried up, 'that the way of the kings of the east might be prepared.'
Kings gathered 'to the place called in the Hebrew tongue Armageddon.'
Seventh vial: 'It is done... there was a great earthquake, such as was not since men were upon the earth.'
'Great Babylon came in remembrance before God, to give unto her the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath.'

characters.name: Babylon the Great and Her Fall
characters.purpose: A vision of 'the great whore' - a woman named Mystery, Babylon the Great, arrayed in purple and scarlet and drunk with the blood of the saints, riding a scarlet beast - followed by her sudden fall and a lament from the kings, merchants, and shipmasters who profited from her, mourning the city's loss 'in one hour.'

verses.note: 'The great whore that sitteth upon many waters,' with whom 'the kings of the earth have committed fornication' - shown to John by an angel explicitly identified as 'one of the seven angels which had the seven vials.'
Seen sitting upon a scarlet-colored beast, 'arrayed in purple and scarlet colour,' holding a golden cup 'full of abominations.'
Name written on her forehead: 'MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.'
'Drunken with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.'
The ten horns and the beast 'shall hate the whore, and shall make her desolate and naked, and shall eat her flesh, and burn her with fire.'
'Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils.'
Kings, merchants, and shipmasters of the earth weep and lament over her destruction.
A mighty angel casts a stone 'like a great millstone' into the sea: 'Thus with violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down, and shall be found no more at all.'

characters.name: The Marriage Supper and the Rider on the White Horse
characters.scribeTier: The Marriage Supper of the Lamb
characters.purpose: Heaven rejoices over Babylon's fall and announces 'the marriage of the Lamb,' with the Church figured as his bride 'arrayed in fine linen, clean and white'; the vision then turns to the triumphant rider on a white horse who defeats the beast, the false prophet, and the kings of the earth gathered against him.

verses.note: A great voice of much people in heaven cries 'Alleluia... for he hath judged the great whore.'
'The marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready... arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints.'
'Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb'; the same angel guiding this vision since 17:1 instructs John to write, and corrects him after John attempts to worship him.
Heaven opened, a white horse, its rider 'Faithful and True,' 'clothed with a vesture dipped in blood: and his name is called The Word of God.'
The armies of heaven follow on white horses; 'KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS' is written on his vesture and thigh.
The beast, the kings of the earth, and their armies gather to make war against him; the beast and false prophet are taken and 'cast alive into a lake of fire.'
The remnant are slain 'with the sword of him that sat upon the horse.'

characters.name: The Thousand Years and the Great White Throne
characters.purpose: Satan is bound for a thousand years while the martyred faithful reign with Christ; released briefly to deceive the nations one final time before being finally defeated and cast into the lake of fire, the vision closes with the dead of all the ages judged before the great white throne 'according to their works,' out of the books, and out of the book of life.

verses.note: 'I saw thrones, and they sat upon them... and they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years.'
'The rest of the dead lived not again until the thousand years were finished. This is the first resurrection.'
Satan is loosed, deceives 'Gog and Magog,' and gathers them 'to battle... in number as the sand of the sea'; fire from God devours them.
'A great white throne, and him that sat on it, from whose face the earth and the heaven fled away.'
'The dead, small and great, stand before God... judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.'
'The sea gave up the dead which were in it; and death and hell delivered up the dead which were in them.'
'Death and hell were cast into the lake of fire... whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.'

characters.name: The New Heaven, New Earth, and New Jerusalem
characters.purpose: The book's final and highest vision - a new heaven and new earth, God dwelling with men, no more death or sorrow, the holy city New Jerusalem descending 'as a bride adorned for her husband' and described in full architectural detail, a city with no temple or need of sun because God and the Lamb are its light - closing with the river and tree of life and the book's own final warnings and benediction. As the closing vision of the entire Bible, it functions as scripture's own capstone: the tree of life, absent since Genesis 3:24, and the presence of God with man, lost at Eden, are both finally and permanently regained.

verses.note: 'A new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away.'
'The holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.'
'God himself shall be with them... God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying.'
'It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.'

An angel explicitly identified as 'one of the seven angels which had the seven vials' carries John away to show him the city: twelve gates named for the twelve tribes of Israel, twelve foundations named for the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
The city is foursquare, measured at twelve thousand furlongs on each side.
'I saw no temple therein: for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it.'
'The city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof.'
'A pure river of water of life... the tree of life, which bare twelve manner of fruits... and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.'
'There shall be no more curse... they shall reign for ever and ever.'
Christ's closing words: 'I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.'
Warning against adding to or taking away from 'the words of the prophecy of this book.'
'Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.'

funFacts: Deliberately built as this project's closing tier for the entire 66-book canon - the tree of life, absent since Genesis 3:24, reappears here as the final book's closing image, and the city's twelve gates and twelve foundations echo the twelve tribes and twelve apostles across both testaments.

characters.name: The Nicolaitans

verses.note: Ephesus is commended: 'thou hatest the deeds of the Nicolaitanes, which I also hate.'
Pergamos is rebuked for tolerating 'them that hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitanes.'

funFacts: Named as a group in two of the seven letters; the text mentions them alongside the doctrine of Balaam without stating explicitly that their teaching is identical to his.

characters.name: Balaam (referenced)

verses.note: Pergamos is rebuked for those who hold 'the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel.'

characters.perkNote: Already indexed as a full character in Numbers.json (Balaam and Balak's oracles, Numbers 22-25, 31:16) - this is a later reference back to that same OT figure, not a new character.

characters.name: Jezebel of Thyatira

verses.note: 'That woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess,' teaches and seduces the church's servants; her followers are threatened with tribulation and death unless she repents.

characters.perkNote: NAMING COLLISION FLAG: not the same person as Jezebel the wife of King Ahab (1 Kings 16, 18-19, 21; 2 Kings 9), who lived roughly nine centuries earlier. This appears to be the text's own chosen label for a local false teacher/prophetess at Thyatira, not a claim that she is literally the same historical woman.

characters.name: Antipas

verses.note: 'Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth.'

funFacts: The only individually named martyr in the whole book.
characters.perkNote: NAMING COLLISION FLAG: not the same person as Herod Antipas, the tetrarch of Galilee already indexed under Matthew.json (who executed John the Baptist, Matthew 14). This Antipas is a faithful martyr of the church at Pergamos; the shared name is coincidental - the text gives no indication these are the same man, and chronology/role make them unrelated figures.

characters.name: Death and Hell

verses.note: The pale horse's rider is named Death, 'and Hell followed with him.'
'Death and hell delivered up the dead which were in them... death and hell were cast into the lake of fire.'

funFacts: Personified together as a pair in both appearances, never separated into individual action - treated as one collective entry rather than two figures.

characters.name: His Angel (the Prologue's Revealing Angel)

verses.note: Christ's revelation is signified 'by his angel unto his servant John' - the book's opening framing device, introduced before the seven letters even begin.

'The Lord God of the holy prophets sent his angel to shew unto his servants the things which must be shortly done' - the book's closing benediction uses the same unqualified 'his angel' phrasing as 1:1.

characters.perkNote: NAMING/IDENTITY FLAG (split from a previously merged entry on adversarial review): Revelation 1:1 and 22:6 both refer only to 'his angel,' without the 'seven vials' qualifier the text uses elsewhere (17:1, 21:9). Kept as a separate entry from the seven-vials angel below because the text itself never explicitly equates them - though the two may well be the same being, that identity is not textually asserted, so it is not asserted here either.

characters.name: One of the Seven Angels with the Seven Vials

verses.note: 'One of the seven angels which had the seven vials talked with me, saying, Come hither; I will shew unto thee the judgment of the great whore.'
Continuing the same vision begun at 17:1, the angel instructs John to write and corrects him after John attempts to worship him.
'One of the seven angels which had the seven vials... talked with me, saying, Come hither, I will shew thee the bride, the Lamb's wife' - explicitly re-identified by the same title as 17:1.
Continuing the vision begun at 21:9, John again attempts to worship the angel and is corrected a second time.

funFacts: Explicitly identified by the same descriptive title - 'one of the seven angels which had the seven vials' - at both 17:1 and 21:9, a real textual marker distinguishing this figure from the unspecified 'his angel' of 1:1/22:6.
Guides John through two of the book's major closing visions: the judgment of Babylon (17:1-19:10) and the vision of the New Jerusalem (21:9-22:9).

genealogyLists.note: Bulk or deliberately-unresolved references, kept out of the character list above.

twelve_tribes_of_the_144000.note: Lists Juda, Reuben, Gad, Aser, Nepthalim, Manasses, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zabulon, Joseph, Benjamin - 12,000 sealed from each. Notably omits Dan from the usual twelve-tribe roster and lists both Joseph and Manasses without a separate Ephraim entry - a real variation from typical OT tribal lists, flagged rather than smoothed over.

gog_and_magog_revelation.note: Reuses the Gog/Magog imagery originally from Ezekiel 38-39 (Old Testament), here applied to a final end-times gathering of the nations rather than repeating that earlier, specific historical setting.

moses_and_elijah_speculation.note: Popular tradition links the Two Witnesses to Moses and Elijah based on the fire-from-mouth, rain-stopping, and water-to-blood parallels to their OT ministries - the text itself never names the two witnesses, so this is logged as tradition, not a textual identification.

jesus_earthly_genealogy.note: Jesus's human genealogy is not restated in Revelation, which gives him only titles ('Root of David,' 'Lion of the tribe of Juda,' 'the root and the offspring of David') rather than a genealogical list - the actual genealogy remains indexed under Matthew.json.

antipas_vs_herod_antipas.note: Antipas, the martyr of Pergamos (Rev 2:13), and Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and executioner of John the Baptist (already indexed under Matthew.json), are two unrelated men who happen to share a name - logged here for cross-reference visibility, not because they are the same figure.
